notes.meaning: The book opens by tracing the line of human history from the very beginning. The writer leaves out Cain and Abel and names Seth, moving in a direct line through godly ancestors to Lamech. By starting with Adam, the Bible reminds us that God is the Creator and Lord of all people, not just one nation.

Noah and his three sons survived the great flood to make a fresh start for humanity. All three sons are named because all the nations of the world grew out of their families. Shem is listed first because the family of Abraham and Jesus would later come through his line.

These verses list the descendants of Japheth, who spread out to become the nations of Europe and northern Asia. Javan is connected with the Greeks, while others settled islands like Cyprus and Rhodes. The writer begins with these distant peoples before turning to the nations closer to Israel's story.

Ham's family included peoples who settled in North Africa, Arabia, and the land of Canaan. Mizraim is the Bible's regular name for Egypt, and Put is linked with Libya. Raamah's sons, Sheba and Dedan, became well-known trading peoples in Arabia.

Nimrod stands out as a grandson of Ham who gained great power and influence. Early traditions and commentators describe him as an arrogant ruler who set up kingdoms like Babylon in defiance of God. His life shows how quickly human power can turn into rebellion against the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that Nimrod's father Cush was originally a different figure from Ham's son Cush, because Nimrod's territory is connected with Mesopotamia rather than Africa.

notes.meaning: Mizraim's descendants formed various tribes and peoples in and around Egypt and North Africa. Among them were the Casluhites and Caphtorites, who were connected to the island of Crete and gave rise to the Philistines. The Philistines would later become one of Israel's closest and most persistent rivals.

Canaan was the father of the peoples who lived in the Promised Land before Israel arrived. Sidon was an ancient and famous seaport city in the north, and Heth was the forefather of the Hittites. Groups like the Jebusites and Amorites were well-known tribes that lived in Canaan.

These verses finish the list of Canaanite clans that settled throughout the land. Many of these names describe whole tribes or city settlements rather than single individuals. Over time, several of these smaller groups blended into neighbouring nations and lost their separate identities.

Shem's family includes nations like Elam, Assyria, and the Arameans or Syrians. The last four names were grandsons through Aram, listed here under Shem's broader family line. Even though many of these powerful nations later conquered or exiled Israel, God was still in charge of their beginnings and their history.

The family line of Shem continues down to Eber through Shelah. The name Eber is widely understood as the root for the word Hebrew. This narrow line carried the special promises of God down toward Abraham and his descendants.

Peleg received his name, which means division, because the people of the earth were separated during his lifetime. Most commentators understand this as the scattering of people into different languages and lands at the tower of Babel. It can also refer to the split between Eber's family lines as Joktan's clan moved away into southern Arabia.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teach that the earth being divided in Peleg's day refers to the physical splitting of the continents rather than the division of languages at Babel.

notes.meaning: Joktan had many sons who went on to settle the southern parts of the Arabian peninsula. Places like Hazarmaveth became known as important trade areas in that region. God tracked each of these families even as they spread far across the ancient world.

The list of Joktan's thirteen sons finishes with Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. Lands like Ophir and Havilah later became famous in the Bible for their rich resources, especially gold. These names remind us how ancient peoples and lands were tied together from the earliest days.

The writer repeats the direct line of Shem to highlight the family through which God's promises would flow. He passes over the other nations to trace the family down from Arphaxad to Reu. God keeps His focus on the narrow lineage that leads to the covenant family.

The genealogy reaches its goal with Abram, whose name God later changed to Abraham. Out of all the families on earth, God called this one man to be the father of the chosen people and the father of all who have faith. Through his family line, God would eventually bring Jesus the Messiah into the world.
